title: Pie-Mary

jokes.text: This is the Lady Gaga of scavenger hunts. A complete work of genius wrapped up in a disorienting mix of confusing cultural red herrings.
jokes.setup: The organizer is hyping up how difficult and brilliant their scavenger hunt is.
jokes.punchline: Comparing their civic scavenger hunt to Lady Gaga — an absurdly self-congratulatory and oddly specific cultural reference that reveals the creator's delusion.
jokes.explanation: The self-important comparison to Lady Gaga is funny character comedy — this person is so proud of their puzzle design that they reach for a pop cultural reference that reveals their total disconnect. The specificity ('disorienting mix of confusing cultural red herrings') adds a layer. Competent setup for the scene's joke about Ron solving it instantly.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's like Lady Gaga, but instead of being born that way, you have to earn it through a series of increasingly difficult challenges that test your wit, your physical endurance, and your ability to follow cryptic clues written in iambic pentameter.

jokes.text: Ron solves the supposedly impossible scavenger hunt in under 30 seconds by rattling off 'columnar transposition,' 'latitude and longitude,' and 'accessing my mental sexton.'
jokes.setup: The organizer has bragged that their hunt received 5/5 Sherlock pipes from the Indiana Puzzlers' Guild and is nearly unsolvable.
jokes.punchline: Ron solves it almost immediately with a calm, clinical explanation that makes the organizer's pride look absurd.
jokes.explanation: This is excellent character comedy. Ron's immediate, effortless destruction of something another person built their entire identity around is perfectly on-brand. The phrase 'accessing my mental sexton' is a wonderfully absurd piece of Ron-speak — a sexton is a real navigational instrument, and calling it 'mental' is both plausible for Ron and ridiculous. The structure is tight: big buildup, instant deflation. High character integration because only Ron could deliver this with such serene indifference. Justifies the near-8 craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I've cross-referenced the latitude and longitude coordinates with the municipal zoning records, triangulated the electromagnetic interference patterns, and decoded the stenographic cipher embedded in the historical land survey. The treasure is buried 47 feet northeast of the old courthouse, approximately 3 feet beneath the water table.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ron, that's... that's not even close to what I—

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm done. I'm leaving.

jokes.text: Keep it. And don't feel bad. It's my curse.
jokes.setup: The organizer is devastated that their masterwork was solved in seconds.
jokes.punchline: Ron responds with total serenity and a hint of tragic self-awareness — being supremely competent is a burden he carries.
jokes.explanation: Peak Ron Swanson economy. Three short sentences do enormous work: he's generous (keep it), he's empathetic (don't feel bad), and he's profoundly self-mythologizing (it's my curse). The joke is that Ron's 'curse' of being too excellent is delivered with complete sincerity as if it's a genuine hardship. Extremely high character integration and economy — this line belongs to Ron and only Ron, and it uses almost no words. Strong quotability. Justifies the 8+ craft score.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I have a gift. It's a curse.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I can see the pattern immediately. The way the colors mesh, the geometric logic. I didn't ask for this.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Most people, they get to enjoy puzzles. Me? I solve them in seconds and I'm left with nothing but the terrible knowledge of what I've done.

jokes.text: Ooh, shop talk. One of my five favorite types of talk, along with pillow, girl, real, and TED.
jokes.setup: Ben suggests they talk shop about the campaign schedule.
jokes.punchline: Leslie rattles off a taxonomy of talk types that perfectly encapsulates her earnest, enthusiastic, pop-culture-savvy personality.
jokes.explanation: The list format is perfectly Leslie — she's made a ranked mental taxonomy of talk types, which is obsessive and charming. 'TED' slotted in alongside 'pillow' and 'girl' talk is the precise comedic payoff; it's unexpected but totally coherent for her character. Strong character integration, good economy. A crowd-pleaser that rewards Leslie fans.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Okay, so there's shop talk, pillow talk, trash talk, small talk, baby talk, sweet talk, pep talk, chalk talk, walk and talk, and TED talks.

jokes.text: Why are you wearing a poncho? Oh, because every surface area in your house is sticky. Last time I was here, I found a melted crayon on my blazer.
jokes.setup: Jen has arrived at Leslie's house wearing a full poncho, an odd choice that demands explanation.
jokes.punchline: It's a defensive measure against the chaos of Leslie's household with three young kids — a completely logical but absurd precaution.
jokes.explanation: Good observational comedy about the reality of toddler-dominated homes. The poncho is a great visual gag (inferred), and 'every surface area is sticky' is a relatable, sharply economical parenting truth. The melted crayon callback grounds it in a specific, funny detail. Works well as character comedy for Jen as a pragmatic, no-nonsense operator.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: The Knope household is a disaster zone of kid mess

jokes.text: Looks like we're gonna have to skip the pie baking event and the ceremonial squash toss. Oh, really? We have to skip that? I love watching those squashes fly through the air. I kind of like the way they land.
jokes.setup: Jen is cutting events from the campaign schedule for practical reasons.
jokes.punchline: Both Leslie and Ben get briefly wistful about the squash toss — a completely absurd local tradition — revealing their genuine love of Pawnee's weird civic culture.
jokes.explanation: A gentle, warm joke about Ben and Leslie's shared affection for Pawnee's absurd traditions. 'I kind of like the way they land' is a nice deadpan beat from Ben — he has a specific, slightly strange appreciation for squash physics. Not a huge laugh but an endearing character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I can't believe we're missing the ceremonial squash toss. I've been practicing my throw all week.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I know, I've been mentally visualizing the perfect arc of a squash in flight.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Right? The way it rotates, the way it tumbles through the air...

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: The satisfying thud when it hits the ground. Why are we like this?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I don't know, but we need to find another squash tossing event immediately.

jokes.text: I already made my pump up mix. There's a surprising amount of Pat Benatar.
jokes.setup: Ben asks Leslie if she's ready for the campaign to get intense.
jokes.punchline: Leslie has, of course, already made a preparedness playlist, and its disproportionate Pat Benatar content is a specific, funny detail.
jokes.explanation: 'A surprising amount of Pat Benatar' is a perfect Leslie detail — it's both specific and slightly inexplicable, which is the sweet spot for her character quirks. The self-aware qualifier 'surprising' is funny because Leslie herself seems mildly puzzled by her own playlist. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Are you ready for intense campaigning?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, I've been listening to my pump-up music all morning.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What kind of pump-up music?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Pat Benatar. All Pat Benatar. Love is a Battlefield, Heartbreaker, Love's a Weapon...

jokes.text: Ben is confused — he says 'I was talking to Leslie' and Leslie says 'Me, Leslie? Yeah.'
jokes.setup: Jen says 'you ready?' and Leslie jumps in confidently, assuming she's being addressed.
jokes.punchline: Ben clarifies he was asking Leslie (the candidate), not Leslie (his wife), and Leslie's slightly deflated 'Me, Leslie?' reveals she briefly forgot which role she was in.
jokes.explanation: A small but functional comedic beat about the confusion of Leslie's dual role (past candidate, current spouse). The setup and payoff are a bit predictable but it lands as a light character moment.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Are you ready for campaigning?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Me? Yeah, I think so.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: I was talking to Leslie.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Oh.

jokes.text: If you were just a ding-dong, I would just slap a flag pin on you, and pour some Valium down your throat. Everything would be fine. It's the smarties that freak people out.
jokes.setup: Jen is explaining the political problem with Leslie being too smart and engaged as a candidate's wife.
jokes.punchline: Her breezy description of the ideal candidate's wife — chemically sedated and accessorized — is a scathing, darkly funny indictment of political optics culture.
jokes.explanation: Jen's brutal political pragmatism is perfectly captured here. 'Slap a flag pin on you and pour some Valium down your throat' is vivid and darkly funny — it's the frank cynicism of someone who operates entirely in outcomes. 'Ding-dong' is a great word choice, casual and dismissive. High character integration for Jen and strong quotability. Justifies the 7.6 craft.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: You know what the real challenge is? Making sure your spouse doesn't overshadow you. Leslie's so smart, so capable... I mean, we'd have to drug her or something to keep her from taking over the whole campaign.

jokes.text: I think you're underestimating the voters. I don't think that is possible.
jokes.setup: Leslie pushes back on Jen's cynicism by defending the intelligence of the electorate.
jokes.punchline: Jen's flat, absolute rebuttal — 'I don't think that is possible' — delivers maximum contempt in minimum words.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully economical joke. Seven words of total voter contempt delivered as a calm, reasonable statement. Jen's character is defined by this kind of flat political nihilism, so it's strong character integration. The structure is classic setup/punchline: Leslie offers an idealistic defense, Jen's reply closes it with a door slam. High quotability — this line travels.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: Being a candidate's wife is like awkward freshman college sex.

dialogue.speaker: Ann Perkins
dialogue.line: You're not sure what you're doing, nobody's really happy, and it's over way too soon.

jokes.text: You know, why don't you think of it like sex freshman year of college? You just want to get through it as fast as possible without embarrassing yourself.
jokes.setup: Jen is trying to explain to Leslie that being a candidate's wife is a minefield.
jokes.punchline: Her analogy — comparing political spousal duty to awkward, rushed freshman sex — is unexpectedly crude and perfectly on-brand for Jen's results-at-all-costs personality.
jokes.explanation: Jen drops this analogy so casually that the shock registers before the logic does — then the logic lands perfectly. It's a good comedic inversion: the professional political consultant reframes civic duty in purely carnal/survival terms. The self-awareness of the explanation ('I'm using that as an analogy to help you out') adds another layer.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, I had a very active college sex life. I was very sexually adventurous. I did things that would make a sorority girl blush.

jokes.text: I'm using that as an analogy to help you out because I'm assuming you were a late bloomer. Not me. I crushed it from day one.
jokes.setup: Jen clarifies her sex-as-analogy, then casually adds a self-assessment.
jokes.punchline: Jen's unprompted, utterly confident sexual self-assessment ('I crushed it from day one') is a perfect Jen non sequitur — ruthlessly competitive even about this.
jokes.explanation: The additional beat — where Jen clarifies she personally was not a late bloomer and 'crushed it from day one' — is the funnier part of the exchange. Jen's competitive nature extends to every domain. The matter-of-fact delivery makes it land harder than a more performed brag would. Strong character integration and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Poncho!

jokes.text: I know you normally hate foundations, but this one I think you'll actually like... Well, I had hoped you'd choose a more dignified trade like masonry or logging.
jokes.setup: April tells Ron about her new job at a foundation that does good work around the world, expecting pushback.
jokes.punchline: Ron's alternative career suggestions — masonry and logging — are perfect Ron values: physical, honest, solitary labor. His framing of a prestigious nonprofit job as undignified compared to logging is a beautiful character inversion.
jokes.explanation: Strongly character-integrated Ron humor. Masonry and logging as aspirational careers for his protégé are hilariously specific and coherent within Ron's worldview. 'More dignified trade' is the key ironic inversion — Ron genuinely means it, which makes it funnier than if he were joking. The follow-up ('But you are out of local government, and that's a step in the right direction') extends the joke well.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: A foundation? That's just a bunch of rich people giving away money they didn't earn. At least manual labor has dignity.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: But I suppose it's better than working for the government.

jokes.text: But you are out of local government, and that's a step in the right direction.
jokes.setup: Ron has just pseudo-criticized April's new job.
jokes.punchline: His silver lining is that she's leaving government — which is, to Ron, genuinely the most important positive outcome regardless of what the job is.
jokes.explanation: Pure Ron Swanson. His anti-government conviction is so deep that 'leaving government' is more valuable to him than the specific merits of April's new opportunity. The line is a consistent expression of Ron's character philosophy, delivered as genuine encouragement. High character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I'm going to miss you. But before you go, I need you to return your office key, parking pass, and municipal ID badge.

jokes.text: If you intend to move, I suppose you should return the spare key to my house... Good talk.
jokes.setup: April reveals she's moving to Washington, D.C. Ron has a quiet emotional reaction to losing a person he clearly cares about deeply.
jokes.punchline: Rather than expressing any emotion, Ron pivots to the practical matter of key retrieval. 'Good talk' closes the exchange with Ron's signature emotional deflection.
jokes.explanation: Ron's emotional armor is perfectly deployed here. The key request is a cover for genuine feeling — and the audience knows it. 'Good talk' after a conversation where almost nothing personal was said is deeply characteristic of Ron. This is the kind of moment that gives Parks and Rec its warmth alongside the comedy. High character integration and economy. Also sets up the episode's A-plot.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter/Dad
dialogue.line: You know, when you think about it, the whole 'Pie Mary' contest is pretty sexist. We're literally naming a baking competition after a woman's name and expecting women to compete in it. It's ridiculous.

jokes.text: Last contest's loser was all women.
jokes.setup: A reporter has just explained the Pie Mary tradition, including the previous winner's recipe.
jokes.punchline: The deadpan observation that the 'loser' of a competition requiring women to perform domestic labor is all women — i.e., the institution itself is the loss — lands as sharp feminist critique disguised as a straight news report.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Eight words do the work of an essay. The structure is a classic misdirection: the setup primes us to hear about the previous loser (a person), and the punchline reveals the loser is a systemic category (all women). Delivered as a matter-of-fact news report, the deadpan register makes it hit harder. Extremely high quotability and economy. Justifies the 8.0 craft score — this is the kind of line that gets clipped and shared.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: The winner of this year's Pie Mary contest is... well, it's a woman. Because apparently only women can make pies. Which is sexist.

jokes.text: Mike Patterson here. Leslie, you made it pretty clear that you don't think homemaking is important. Do you ever cook for your children? And who's even watching your children right now while you're out God only knows where?
jokes.setup: Ben is giving an economic address; Leslie is standing right there, visible to Mike.
jokes.punchline: 'What are you talking about? I'm standing right here in front of you' — the absurdity of a reporter asking where someone is while looking directly at them encapsulates the media's bad faith in covering women in politics.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed cringe comedy moment that functions as satire. Each question Mike asks escalates the absurdity ('who's even watching your children right now') until the punchline that she's literally standing in front of him deflates his manufactured outrage beautifully. Works on the comedy and political satire levels simultaneously.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: So Leslie, with all your time spent on these various projects, who's watching your kids right now?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: They're at home with a babysitter.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: And where are you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: I'm right here. At this event. Literally in front of you.

jokes.text: Okay, take it easy. Let's not get emotional.
jokes.setup: Leslie calmly and accurately points out that she's standing right in front of Mike.
jokes.punchline: Mike tells Leslie not to get emotional — when she's the calmest person in the scene and he's the one who has been performing outrage.
jokes.explanation: A sharp ironic beat — the classic 'don't get emotional' dismissal deployed against someone who is demonstrably not being emotional. Works well in context as part of the escalating satire of how media treats women candidates.

jokes.text: How much did that haircut cost? None of your business. And thank you for noticing.
jokes.setup: A reporter asks Leslie an inappropriate question about her haircut cost in the middle of a political event.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's reply pivots from appropriate boundary-setting ('none of your business') to accidentally genuine vanity ('and thank you for noticing') — a perfectly Leslie response that reveals her inability to resist a compliment, even from a hostile questioner.
jokes.explanation: This is a standout joke in the episode. The setup (rude question) establishes Leslie's correct, firm response. The punchline ('and thank you for noticing') is a perfect character break — Leslie can't help herself. It's both a critique of the question's absurdity AND a revelation of Leslie's personality. Only Leslie Knope would thank someone who was trying to embarrass her, because her love of her own hair overwhelms her sense of indignation. High craft scores across the board. Justifies the 8.2.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Where are your kids while you're out God knows where?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm at a scheduled public event. It's on the calendar.

jokes.text: My desk was right here. Sitting right on top of it this whole time. How much money is it? It's not money. I told you. It's Ron's key.
jokes.setup: April and Andy have been searching for Ron's key which April hid years ago.
jokes.punchline: Andy keeps assuming whatever they're looking for is money — a running character beat that reflects his simplistic worldview.
jokes.explanation: A functional Andy character beat. His assumption that everything is money is a reliable but not especially sophisticated comedic shorthand for his character. Gets a mild smile but not a big laugh.

dialogue.speaker: Mike Patterson
dialogue.line: Why won't you just let me dump this toxic waste in the park?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Because it's illegal, it's dangerous, and it will poison the groundwater that thousands of people depend on.

dialogue.speaker: Mike Patterson
dialogue.line: Wow, there you go again. Being so emotional. Why do you always have to be so emotional about everything?

jokes.text: Just a note and a movie ticket stub and four teeth.
jokes.setup: Andy opens the box looking for Ron's key.
jokes.punchline: The inventory of box contents escalates from mundane (note, ticket stub) to deeply weird (four teeth) — the teeth are the absurdist spike.
jokes.explanation: The escalation to 'four teeth' is perfectly timed and deeply strange in a way that is very April. The list structure sets up the absurdist spike well. This also does triple duty: it's funny on its own, establishes April's character, and sets up later revelations (the teeth turn out to be from Donna's New Moon trip). Good comedic construction.

dialogue.speaker: Mike Patterson
dialogue.line: Isn't it true you spent $400 on a haircut using taxpayer money?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: That is absolutely not true. And also, thank you for noticing.

jokes.text: 'If you are looking for Ron's key, I moved it, and you'll never find it. Cordially, April.' Where'd you put it then? I don't know. It was eight years ago.
jokes.setup: A note from past-April promises that she's hidden the key and they'll never find it.
jokes.punchline: Present-April has absolutely no memory of where she put it — her past self's smug confidence is completely undermined by the passage of time.
jokes.explanation: Excellent structural comedy. The note is written with complete confidence and mild menace ('you'll never find it. Cordially'), and April's confession that she has no idea where she put it perfectly deflates past-April's self-satisfaction. 'Cordially' as a closing for a mischievous note is a great character detail. The time-collapse structure (past April vs. present April) is well-executed.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I found Ron's key in April's hiding spot. Let's see what else is in here...

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Oh, there's a... is that a human tooth?

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, there's another one. And another one.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: April, why do you have a collection of human teeth?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: They're not human.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, well that's somehow worse.

jokes.text: All we gotta do is train Champion to sniff out Ron's key. Okay. All we need is Ron's key to give him a scent. So give me the key and I'll get you that key.
jokes.setup: Andy proposes using their dog Champion to track the key by scent.
jokes.punchline: His plan immediately hits a circular logical problem (you need the key to find the key) that he doesn't register as a problem.
jokes.explanation: Andy's circular logic is well-constructed — the setup builds to a confident 'give me the key and I'll get you that key' that is completely oblivious to its own impossibility. Character integration is strong (this is Andy's brand of earnest, well-meaning incompetence).

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: If you're reading this, you've found my key. Good job, detective. Return it immediately or I will find you and make you regret ever being born. Cordially, April Ludgate.

jokes.text: Well, it only took three hours for Jen to be right.
jokes.setup: Leslie is watching a TV news segment that has already turned the Pie Mary skip into a feminist controversy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's defeated, matter-of-fact acknowledgment that Jen's cynical prediction came true almost immediately.
jokes.explanation: A functional callback that pays off Jen's earlier cynicism. Leslie's defeated, self-aware delivery makes it land. Not a huge joke but a good structural beat.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, so we need to find the key, right? But to find the key, we need the key to unlock where the key is hidden. Which means we need the key to find the key.

jokes.text: Besides, I'm good at making pies, so I'll win and then I can promote my self-published women's rights barbecue cookbook The Feminine Mesquite.
jokes.setup: Leslie decides to enter the Pie Mary and is explaining why it's actually fine.
jokes.punchline: 'The Feminine Mesquite' — a pun on Betty Friedan's 'The Feminine Mystique,' applied to a BBQ cookbook — is exactly the kind of thing Leslie would write and be proud of.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. The Feminine Mesquite is a perfect character artifact: it combines Leslie's feminism, her policy nerdiness, her love of Pawnee traditions (BBQ), and her tendency to over-complicate everything into a single self-published object. The pun itself is good — mesquite/mystique is close enough to land — but what elevates it is that it's entirely believable. You can picture the cover. The fact that she's already written and self-published it is the funnier part. Justifies the 8.3 craft score.

dialogue.speaker: June Hartwell
dialogue.line: Leslie Knope didn't show up to the pie contest. She just... didn't come.

dialogue.speaker: Reporter
dialogue.line: Do you know why?

dialogue.speaker: June Hartwell
dialogue.line: No idea. But I'm going to assume it's because she's lazy and doesn't care about Pawnee.

jokes.text: Everything's fine. Except you're gonna need to get a new calculator 'cause I crushed this one in a blind rage while I was watching the show.
jokes.setup: Leslie confidently declares 'everything's fine.'
jokes.punchline: The immediately following qualifier reveals that her 'blind rage' — contradicting the 'fine' claim — expressed itself through an act of appliance destruction that she's now casually disclosing.
jokes.explanation: The structure is excellent: 'everything's fine' is the false claim, and 'except I crushed a calculator in blind rage' is the immediate self-contradiction. The word 'crushed' (not broke, not threw — crushed) implies something about the force of Leslie's feelings. The calm delivery of this disclosure is key. Very Leslie: processing intense emotion through mild property damage and then immediately moving on.

jokes.text: I found this one, but it has a falcon on the top. I'll keep looking. No, that's it! That's it, Andy! Eagle, falcon, whatever. Not whatever. Eagles are more robust, have stronger talents. Didn't go to Bird School much?
jokes.setup: They're looking for a specific box with an eagle on top; Andy found one with a falcon.
jokes.punchline: Ron-proxy April corrects Andy on the eagle/falcon distinction with the line 'Didn't go to Bird School much?' — a profoundly absurd Ron-ism that April has apparently internalized.
jokes.explanation: 'Didn't go to Bird School much?' is an absurdist gem — 'Bird School' is not a real institution but April delivers it as if it's an obvious credential gap. The detail that eagles have 'stronger talents' (she means talons, which is also a funny slip OR intentional) adds to the joke. April doing a Ron impression is always funny because of how much she's absorbed his sensibility.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Yeah, well, Jen called that one pretty fast.

jokes.text: Garry's wedding ring, Tom's watch, Kyle's car keys...
jokes.setup: They open the box expecting Ron's key and find a collection of other people's valuables.
jokes.punchline: April has been hoarding the personal items of her colleagues for years — a revealing inventory that recontextualizes past events. The escalating list implies a comprehensive program of theft/retrieval.
jokes.explanation: The list is a great character reveal — April has been systematically collecting coworkers' lost items for years, apparently as some combination of dark hobby and voodoo preparation (as confirmed by the next beat). The escalating specificity (each item belongs to a named character) rewards attentive viewers.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm going to win this pie contest, and then I'll have the perfect platform to promote my weirdly specific feminist BBQ cookbook.

jokes.text: Wait, wait. I lost that wedding ring down the sewer grate six years ago. I know. And I fished it out, so I can put it on my voodoo doll.
jokes.setup: Garry recognizes his wedding ring in April's collection and recalls losing it down a sewer grate.
jokes.punchline: April retrieved it specifically to use on a voodoo doll — a casually dark reveal that she's been conducting a years-long occult campaign against Garry.
jokes.explanation: This is a great April joke. The structure is perfect: Garry's recollection of losing the ring is a setup, and April's flat explanation that she retrieved it for a voodoo doll is a maximally unexpected punchline. 'So I can put it on my voodoo doll' is delivered with complete normalcy — April doesn't think this needs explanation. The specificity of 'put it ON my voodoo doll' (not just 'for a voodoo doll') implies the doll already exists and is operational. Justifies the 8.1 craft.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Everything's fine with the campaign. I'm just going to go back to my office and calmly file some paperwork.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: AHHHHH!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie? Are you okay?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: FINE! EVERYTHING'S FINE!

jokes.text: Garry, goodbye. We're disappearing forever. You're a nice man and I'm sorry for everything I did to you. Goodbye.
jokes.setup: April and Andy realize the key isn't in the box and are at a momentary dead end.
jokes.punchline: April's immediate solution is to say a heartfelt goodbye to Garry and vanish forever — treating this minor setback as an occasion to disappear rather than face the consequences.
jokes.explanation: The joke works on multiple levels: April's extreme flight response, the unexpected warmth of 'you're a nice man,' and the implicit confession of long-term workplace torment ('sorry for everything I did to you'). The apology is both genuinely touching and funny in its vagueness — 'everything' implies a lot. Very April.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, this isn't an eagle box?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: It's a falcon box.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: What's the difference?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Did you go to Bird School?

jokes.text: Initiate Ghost Protocol. We switch faces, we burn our fingertips off with acid, we live in the tunnels beneath the Kremlin. We could do that easily.
jokes.setup: April wants to run away from the key problem. Andy considers the option seriously.
jokes.punchline: Andy has a detailed, operational spy-movie escape plan ready — and insists 'we could do that easily' as if it's a genuine alternative.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'switch faces' to 'burn our fingertips off with acid' to 'tunnels beneath the Kremlin' is well-calibrated — each step is more extreme. 'We could do that easily' is the button, delivered with Andy's characteristic confidence in absurd plans. Strong Andy character voice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I retrieved your wedding ring from the sewer. I'm using it for my voodoo doll of you.

jokes.text: We could easily go that route. Initiate Ghost Protocol. We switch faces, we burn our fingertips off with acid, we live in the tunnels beneath the Kremlin. We could do that easily. But this is not that big of a deal.
jokes.setup: April suggests they just run away and disappear rather than tell Ron about the lost key.
jokes.punchline: Andy fully endorses the disappearance plan, elaborating on the logistics (face-switching, acid fingertips, Kremlin tunnels) with complete earnestness before casually noting it's not necessary.
jokes.explanation: The escalation is well-paced: Ghost Protocol → face-switching → acid fingertips → Kremlin tunnels. Each step is more absurd. The comedic pivot ('but this is not that big of a deal') after fully committing to a spy-movie escape plan is the perfect Andy beat — he could go either way on this, and he's genuinely indifferent. Very strong character integration: Andy lives in a movie universe where any of this is a reasonable option.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I'm just going to run away.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Okay, I've actually been prepared for this. I have an entire spy movie escape plan ready to go. We rappel down the side of the building, we hot-wire a car, we drive to the airport, we steal a plane, and we fly to a non-extradition country.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's... actually not a terrible plan.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know. I've been working on it since high school.

jokes.text: Garry, I take everything back. I hate you.
jokes.setup: April just said a heartfelt goodbye to Garry and expressed genuine affection.
jokes.punchline: Andy talks her out of running away, and her first act of returning to normalcy is immediately retracting her kind words to Garry.
jokes.explanation: An excellent callback with perfect structure. April's rare moment of emotional openness is immediately revoked, maintaining her character consistency while making the brief warmth even funnier in retrospect. 'I take everything back. I hate you.' is maximally economical — six words that perfectly cap the sequence. The fact that Garry presumably just accepts this without protest adds another comedic layer. Justifies the 8.0.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Goodbye, Garry. That was nice.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: You're still a idiot though.

jokes.text: An impossible puzzle. And I love puzzles.
jokes.setup: Ron is being told that April accidentally created an unsolvable multi-clue mystery.
jokes.punchline: Ron's reaction is not annoyance or disappointment — it's quiet, predatory delight. This is his natural habitat.
jokes.explanation: Three words of pure Ron: the comma-pause between the admission (it's impossible) and his reaction (he loves that) is perfect comedic rhythm. This calls back to the opening scene where he instantly solved the Puzzlers' Guild hunt. The contrast — a complicated puzzle that stymied Ron vs. one that finally challenges him — is satisfying and character-rich.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: What is this? 'Twilight'? These are just pictures of shirtless men sparkling in the sun. This is the worst thing that's ever been made. It's poorly written, it's poorly acted, and the whole thing just reeks of desperation and bad choices.

jokes.text: These appear to be human teeth. And what is this? New Moon? It's a movie, but I've never seen it.
jokes.setup: Ron is examining the box's contents as clues: a note, a movie ticket, and teeth.
jokes.punchline: Ron's inventory is delivered with the same analytical calm whether he's examining latitude/longitude or human teeth. His complete unfazedness by the teeth, followed by unfamiliarity with a wildly popular film, is a great Ron character double.
jokes.explanation: Ron treating human teeth as a routine puzzle element is funny. His unfamiliarity with Twilight (possibly the most culturally pervasive film franchise at that moment) is expected but delivered well. The double comes from the inversion: he's unbothered by the strange (teeth) and oblivious to the mainstream (Twilight).

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is the greatest puzzle I've ever encountered.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's just a Rubik's Cube.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I solved it in under a minute. This one... this one has layers.

jokes.text: It's, like, about lame werewolves and vampires and stuff. Donna likes those things. Dollars to donuts this points us her way.
jokes.setup: Ron is trying to identify what the New Moon ticket stub means as a clue.
jokes.punchline: Andy dismisses Twilight as 'lame werewolves and stuff,' and Ron immediately uses this dismissal as deductive reasoning to point toward Donna — associating Donna's known tastes with the evidence.
jokes.explanation: 'Dollars to donuts' is a funny anachronistic phrase from Ron, and his use of Donna's Twilight fandom as deductive evidence is a good character beat. Andy's review of the franchise ('lame werewolves and vampires and stuff') is also a reliable joke. Functional and light.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I put the kids to bed last night. First, Ella wanted me to read her a story, so I read her 'Charlotte's Web.' She cried for twenty minutes because the pig dies. Then I had to explain that the pig doesn't actually die, he just grows up and becomes bacon.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Then Ramsés wanted me to help him with his science project. It's due tomorrow. Tomorrow! We ended up building a volcano out of papier-mâché at 11 PM while I'm explaining how lava works.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Then I couldn't find Nora for like fifteen minutes. I'm panicking, checking the closets, the cabinets. I finally found her in the backyard climbing a tree at midnight in her pajamas. When I asked her what she was doing, she said 'Looking for the moon.'

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I don't know how that works. I don't know how any of this works.

jokes.text: kids tucked in, books read, three simultaneous meltdowns for no reason, kids tucked back in, one of them briefly got outside somehow
jokes.setup: Ben is narrating his solo childcare operation while Leslie handles the Pie Mary crisis.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of chaotic events — three simultaneous meltdowns, then one child 'briefly got outside somehow' — is a perfectly specific, absurd portrait of toddler parenthood. 'Somehow' is the key word.
jokes.explanation: A great parenting joke hiding in a brief throwaway. The structure is an understated list that escalates to absurdity: 'three simultaneous meltdowns' is funny, but 'one of them briefly got outside somehow' is the spike. 'Somehow' implies both that Ben doesn't know HOW and that he's made peace with not knowing. Highly relatable and sharply written.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: I brought baking supplies.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh my god, is that whipped cream?

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Don't even think about it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: I'm just going to have a little bit.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: Leslie, no. We need that for the recipe.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: One tiny taste won't hurt.

dialogue.speaker: Ann
dialogue.line: You're going to eat the entire can straight, aren't you?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Probably.

jokes.text: I even got an extra whipped cream can, one for baking, one for directly into mouth.
jokes.setup: Ben is triumphantly presenting his pie-baking supply haul.
jokes.punchline: The second whipped cream can is explicitly for direct consumption, not baking — a casual admission of a very relatable vice, delivered as a perfectly normal logistical note.
jokes.explanation: The two-can whipped cream system is a great bit. The parallel structure ('one for baking, one for directly into mouth') is clean and the matter-of-fact acknowledgment of the mouth-can's purpose is the joke. Ben's fandom of food is a consistent character trait this pays off.

dialogue.speaker: Elise
dialogue.line: I'm going to protest Leslie at the pie event. I'm going to throw a pie right in her face.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Wait, you're actually going to throw a pie at me?

dialogue.speaker: Elise
dialogue.line: No, no, it's metaphorical. I'm going to protest her policies, not literally pie her in the face.

jokes.text: Are you here to give me the Woman of the Year award? I have a speech prepared. Would you like to see it? Right now? No.
jokes.setup: A visitor shows up at Leslie's door, and Leslie immediately jumps to the best possible interpretation.
jokes.punchline: Her assumption (Woman of the Year award delivery) and the instant speech offer is a perfect capsule of Leslie's self-aware-yet-still-hopeful grandiosity. Elise's flat 'No' is the straight-man punchline.
jokes.explanation: A great Leslie joke. Her immediate leap to the most flattering interpretation (award delivery!), followed by the reveal that she has a speech ready even for this hypothetical, is very on-brand. 'Right now? No.' from Elise is a perfect flat response. The joke is economical and the character integration is nearly perfect.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Me want pie. Me want pie now.

jokes.text: Babe, the oven's ready. Chop-chop, time to get bakin'. Daddy want pie.
jokes.setup: Leslie is in the middle of a tense conversation with Elise from the IOW about feminist principles.
jokes.punchline: Ben cheerfully interrupts with urgent domestic energy and the phrase 'Daddy want pie' — completely unaware of the ideological minefield he's wandered into.
jokes.explanation: 'Daddy want pie' is a great cringe comedy beat — Ben's cheerful obliviousness as he calls himself 'Daddy' in a context that makes it maximally unfortunate. The timing (mid-feminist argument) and the visual of Leslie's reaction (implied) make this a strong in-scene joke.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: I missed my seventh viewing because of April's painkiller incident at the Twilight movie.

jokes.text: She was so hopped up on painkillers from getting her wisdom teeth out, I convinced her to see it with me. The teeth. They're yours. You were super out of it. You kept yelling 'Team Voldemort!' at the screen and we were kicked out.
jokes.setup: Ron and Andy are questioning Donna about the New Moon ticket stub and the teeth found in the box.
jokes.punchline: The teeth in April's collection are Donna's wisdom teeth, extracted during a painkiller-induced Twilight outing where she yelled 'Team Voldemort' (from the wrong franchise) and got them ejected.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding callback payoff. The joke has multiple layers: (1) April kept Donna's extracted wisdom teeth, (2) the context for the teeth involves a painkiller-fueled movie outing, (3) the crowning detail is 'Team Voldemort' — a franchise confusion that is perfect for someone in a medicated haze. 'Team Voldemort' is the spike — Voldemort is from Harry Potter, not Twilight, and yelling it at a Twilight film is so specifically wrong it becomes genius. Getting kicked out for it is perfect escalation. The payoff on the teeth setup from earlier justifies the 8.2+ craft.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: Wait, you had a crush on me? Back then?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Yeah, for like two years.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: That's so embarrassing!

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: We're married.

dialogue.speaker: Andy
dialogue.line: I know, but still!

jokes.text: You only get to see the second Twilight film for the seventh time once.
jokes.setup: Donna explains that she was furious about being kicked out of the movie.
jokes.punchline: The joke is that this was Donna's seventh viewing of New Moon, which she treats as a perfectly normal thing — the 'you only get one chance' framing applied to her seventh theatrical viewing is the absurdist inversion.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best lines. The grammatical/logical construction is funny on its own — 'you only get to [do X] for the Nth time once' is technically true of any experience, but applying it to a seventh viewing of a movie makes it simultaneously profound and absurd. It's a perfect encapsulation of Donna's unapologetic, maximalist self-indulgence. The deadpan delivery would elevate it further. Strong economy (twelve words, massive laugh) and near-perfect character integration. Justifies the 8.6.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: I need to get my wedding ring out of the sewer!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Don't worry, Jerry. We'll help you get it back.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: Thank you so much!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: I'll just reach down and... ow! This pipe is hot!

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, move over. I've got this. I'm very flexible.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Oh no, I'm stuck!

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: This is amateur hour. I'll use my tools.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: The sewer main just exploded.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: My ring! And now I have a geyser in my yard!

jokes.text: Babe. You had a crush on me. That's embarrassing. We're married. Still.
jokes.setup: They've learned from Donna that April had a big crush on Andy when she hid the key there.
jokes.punchline: Andy teases April about the crush. April's 'Still.' — acknowledging that the embarrassment is ongoing because they're married — is the perfect deadpan punctuation.
jokes.explanation: Andy's observation ('That's embarrassing') and April's one-word response ('Still') is a beautiful tiny exchange. 'Still' implies that having a crush on someone and then marrying them is inherently embarrassing, and April cannot escape this fact. Maximum economy. This is affectionate writing for a beloved couple.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: You know, I've been watching you work here for a lot of years, Garry. And I gotta say, watching you suffer is the only thing that brings me joy anymore.

jokes.text: To the shoeshine stand! Ooh! Chase me. Stop.
jokes.setup: Ron declares the next destination with dramatic flair; Andy gets excited.
jokes.punchline: Andy immediately starts a chase game; Ron shuts it down with a flat 'Stop.' The contrast between Andy's childlike energy and Ron's zero-tolerance dignity is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A quick, functional character beat. Ron's 'Stop' is delivered as an absolute with no elaboration — he won't dignify Andy's game with an explanation. Reliable Andy/Ron dynamic.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's a circle of dough, it's got cheese, it's got meat, it's got sauce...

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That sounds like a pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, it's not a pizza.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What is it?

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's a calzone.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, that's a pizza folded in half.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, you're in the no-fly zone. The calzone.

jokes.text: Oh, gosh. Well, I dropped my wedding ring down this grate, and then I was trying to get it out and I dropped my keys down there too, so I can't leave.
jokes.setup: Garry is found kneeling at a sewer grate in a comically unfortunate position.
jokes.punchline: Garry has compounded his original mistake (dropping the ring) with an additional mistake (dropping his keys while trying to fix the first), leaving him literally trapped. This is quintessential Garry.
jokes.explanation: The escalating catastrophe is very Garry — each attempted solution creates a worse problem. The fact that he's now trapped is a strong physical comedy premise (inferred visual). The 'Oh, gosh' opener is perfect Garry vocal character work.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Wait, I've got it. What if we just made it a calzone contest instead?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Ben, no. It's a pie contest.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: A calzone is just a folded pie.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: That's not what a calzone is.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Look, I'm not saying change the rules. I'm just saying a calzone would solve this problem.

jokes.text: Mmm. Nuts. Never fear. I still have my passport.
jokes.setup: Garry has just lost his credit card and driver's license into the grate while attempting the chopstick retrieval.
jokes.punchline: 'Nuts' is Garry's peak expletive. And his fallback solution is to use his passport — his last remaining document — as the next improvised tool.
jokes.explanation: The escalation from 'I dropped my ring' to 'I've now destroyed my credit card, driver's license, and am about to sacrifice my passport' is a great Garry catastrophe sequence. 'Nuts' as his strongest available expletive is perfect Garry character comedy. 'Never fear' before proposing an even riskier plan is a great comic beat.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Lana! Lana! LANA!

jokes.text: Wait, let me see your stamps.
jokes.setup: Garry is about to drop his passport into the grate as his next retrieval tool.
jokes.punchline: Donna's only concern about the passport is seeing the travel stamps — completely indifferent to Garry's crisis, interested only in the tourism data.
jokes.explanation: A quick character beat that perfectly establishes Donna's priorities: she is a traveler, she is untroubled by others' crises, and she will get what she wants from any situation. Her flat request to see the stamps is funny in its casual selfishness.

dialogue.speaker: Jerry
dialogue.line: She called me 'Mr. Forgetful' and I've never been so hurt in my life.

jokes.text: Oh, my God, Ben, I gave them $100 in their annual pledge. Do you know how many anti-me signs that could buy? Or even banners.
jokes.setup: Leslie has donated to the IOW, which is now protesting her.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's horror is framed in sign-economics ('how many anti-me signs that could buy'), and then escalated to 'or even banners' — which would be a bigger production value anti-Leslie campaign.
jokes.explanation: Leslie framing her IOW donation in terms of anti-Leslie protest purchasing power is a fun character bit. The escalation to 'or even banners' — which implies she's thought through the materials budget for a protest against herself — is the comedic spike. Good character integration.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: We're not doing anything with it!

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Yeah, we just like having rope in the basement!

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: It's a hobby.

jokes.text: What should we do? Should we get a divorce?
jokes.setup: Leslie and Ben are trying to solve the political problem of the Pie Mary controversy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's escalation from 'this is a political problem' to 'should we get a divorce?' is a perfectly absurd leap — treating a PR crisis as grounds for marital dissolution.
jokes.explanation: A good absurdist escalation. Leslie's problem-solving mechanism, when pushed to the extreme, generates maximally catastrophic solutions as a starting point. The non sequitur divorce option is both funny and revealing of her stressed state.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: We used to play this game in college where you'd choke yourself until you passed out.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: Ah yes, we called it the Henley Maneuver.

jokes.text: And then we flip the antiquated tradition right on its head. Exactly. But more importantly, we change the idea of what a pie is. I feel like that's not more important, but I like the energy that we have, so let's hear it.
jokes.setup: Ben and Leslie are excited about Ben entering the pie contest to flip the tradition. Leslie then escalates to 'more importantly' — reframing what a pie IS.
jokes.punchline: Ben's response ('I feel like that's not more important') gently checks her while still validating her enthusiasm. It's a beautifully calibrated response that is both reasonable and funny.
jokes.explanation: Ben's diplomatic 'I feel like that's not more important, but I like the energy that we have' is a perfect Leslie-handler line. He's managing her enthusiasm without deflating it. The fact that he then immediately goes along with her plan (calzones) makes it funnier in retrospect. Great relationship comedy.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: We share dreams because we're best friends.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: Yeah, and our sleeping arrangement isn't romantic.

dialogue.speaker: Harris
dialogue.line: We're just two guys who love each other.

dialogue.speaker: Brett
dialogue.line: In a completely platonic way.

jokes.text: Okay, picture this... Crust on the bottom. Filling. Crust on top. What am I describing? A pie. No. But you're in the right 'zone.' Oh. Calzone! Sure!
jokes.setup: Leslie is building to a big reveal about what she's going to make instead of a pie.
jokes.punchline: Her dramatic description of a pie is technically describing a calzone, and her 'right zone' hint is a pun. Ben's flat 'Sure!' upon arrival at 'calzone' is the capper.
jokes.explanation: A well-constructed bit. The lead-up (Leslie describing a pie in the most fundamental terms) creates genuine suspense about where she's going, and the 'right zone' pun is groan-inducing in the best way. Ben's enthusiasm-tempered 'Sure!' is the correct reaction from someone supportive but realistic. The calzone solution itself is inherently funny as an act of pie revisionism.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: So let me get this straight. A ghost that only appears on Tuesdays, makes a sound like a sad trombone, and leaves behind the smell of old cheese. That's not a ghost. That's just Ron's basement.

jokes.text: Talking 'bout the highway to the calzone zone
jokes.setup: Ben is energized by the calzone plan.
jokes.punchline: He improvises a song merging 'Highway to the Danger Zone' (Top Gun) with 'calzone zone' — revealing his nerd-dad energy in full.
jokes.explanation: Ben's spontaneous calzone song is a great character moment — he's so excited about the calzone plan that he's already written the anthem. The mash-up of Top Gun with calzone is very Ben Wyatt energy. Highly character-integrated.

dialogue.speaker: Donna
dialogue.line: Well, that's not what Gayle calls it.

jokes.text: I'm having some serious déjà vu. How many times have you lost your wedding ring?
jokes.setup: Donna finds Garry once again dealing with a lost wedding ring situation.
jokes.punchline: The implication that this is a recurring Garry pattern — so frequent that Donna has déjà vu — is the joke.
jokes.explanation: A competent Garry recurring-failure joke. The déjà vu framing works. Not particularly original but consistent with the episode's ongoing Garry thread.

dialogue.speaker: June Hartwell
dialogue.line: I can spell P-I-E.

jokes.text: And any time I lose my ring, she turns into a real grumpy goose. Is that so? Oh, yeah. She'll say, 'Garry, you'd lose your head if it wasn't screwed on tight.' And then she makes me go for the fresh oranges for the morning OJ.
jokes.setup: Garry is describing how his wife Gayle reacts when he loses his ring.
jokes.punchline: Her punishment is sending him for 'fresh oranges for the morning OJ' — a completely benign domestic errand that Garry describes with the gravity of a serious penalty. 'Grumpy goose' is Garry's vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: Garry's vocabulary ('grumpy goose') and the anti-climactic nature of Gayle's punishment (orange-fetching) is funny. The joke is that Garry experiences these benign domestic consequences with the same gravity others would give serious punishments. His characterization as someone with an enviably kind home life despite workplace humiliation is a running show joke.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Ladies and gentlemen, what we have here is not just a calzone. It's a gift. A gift wrapped in a warm, delicious blanket of dough and cheese. This calzone represents the pinnacle of Italian-American cuisine. When you bite into this, you're not just eating food, you're experiencing a moment of pure joy.

jokes.text: She'll say, 'Hey, Mr. Forgetful.' And then those words... they rattle around here for hours.
jokes.setup: Garry is continuing to describe Gayle's mild reproach for losing the ring.
jokes.punchline: Gayle's most severe verbal criticism is 'Mr. Forgetful,' and Garry describes it rattling around in his head — implying profound hurt from something almost laughably gentle.
jokes.explanation: The joke here is the vast disproportion between the gentleness of 'Mr. Forgetful' and Garry's wounded reaction to it. This reinforces the running show joke that Garry's home life is so warm that mildly affectionate teasing counts as a wound. Paired with the earlier 'grumpy goose,' it builds a picture of an almost absurdly loving marriage.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: Men's rights activism is about protecting the fundamental freedoms that men have enjoyed for centuries. Our oppression is very recent.

jokes.text: The shoeshine stand is gone. Or maybe it was never here.
jokes.setup: They've arrived at the shoeshine stand location and it's not there.
jokes.punchline: 'Or maybe it was never here' is April undermining objective reality with casual nihilism, as is her character.
jokes.explanation: A small April character beat. Her willingness to question whether physical objects ever existed is a funny expression of her nihilistic sensibility. Light but character-appropriate.

dialogue.speaker: Talk Show Host
dialogue.line: Well, that's the thing about this controversy - it's one of those rare issues where everyone agrees. Democrats hate it, Republicans hate it, Independents hate it. Even people who don't follow politics hate it.

jokes.text: Do what, exactly? Nothing. We're not doing anything. And we definitely do not live down here now.
jokes.setup: Ron, Andy, and April find the maintenance guys in the basement apparently doing something with a rope.
jokes.punchline: The unprompted denial of living in the basement — before anyone suggested it — implies they do, in fact, live down here now.
jokes.explanation: A classic ironic denial — protesting something no one accused you of immediately confirms it. 'We definitely do not live down here now' is exactly specific enough to be suspicious. Good Harris character beat.

jokes.text: Well, we're on our own quest, which is to squeeze this just tight enough to make my eyes bulge out a little bit, but not so tight that I die. I've been there. That's a real tightrope walk.
jokes.setup: Ron demands answers about the shoeshine stand; the maintenance guys explain what they're doing.
jokes.punchline: They're experimenting with self-strangulation for the eyeball-bulging effect, with Ron confirming he has personal experience with the mortality risk. The absurdity is in the casual normality of the exchange.
jokes.explanation: A beautifully dark absurdist joke. The specificity of the goal ('eyes bulge out a little bit, but not so tight that I die') is very funny — it's a well-defined target. Ron's expert confirmation ('I've been there. That's a real tightrope walk') is both absurd and character-appropriate (Ron would have experimented with this). The exchange treats a dangerous activity as a normal technical challenge.

dialogue.speaker: Ron Swanson
dialogue.line: I find it troubling that men aren't represented on this feminism panel. How can we discuss women's issues without men in charge of the conversation?

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Ron, that's... that's not how this works.

jokes.text: Last week this real scary ghost came down here looking for it. It had black hair, but you could see through his skin. And it wouldn't talk to me. It would only talk to Harris. No, dude. That was just that bonk's dream that I had. How are we gonna have the same dream, dude? 'Cause we're best friends. I love you, dawg. Man, I love you!
jokes.setup: Brett reports that a ghost came looking for the shoeshine stand.
jokes.punchline: Harris clarifies it was his dream, not a real ghost — but Brett's confusion about how they could have the same dream leads to an emotional best-friend declaration.
jokes.explanation: A great Harris/Brett bit. Brett's ghost report is delivered with complete sincerity, and the dream clarification opens a metaphysical question that leads to a sudden emotional declaration of friendship. The logic ('cause we're best friends') as an explanation for shared dreaming is absurdly sweet. These characters are used sparingly and to good effect.

dialogue.speaker: Brandi Maxxxx
dialogue.line: I've been in over 300 films. My most recent work was 'Buttman's Inferno 7,' which I'm very proud of. Before that, I did 'Ass-tronomy' and 'Pulp Friction.'

jokes.text: We're dreaming together / We're sleeping together / But not like that
jokes.setup: Harris and Brett have just declared their love as best friends.
jokes.punchline: They sing/chant a brief song clarifying the nature of their shared-dream friendship — the 'but not like that' disclaimer is the payoff.
jokes.explanation: A brief, silly impromptu song. 'But not like that' is the correct and efficient punchline. The song itself is absurd and character-consistent for Harris and Brett, who seem to operate in their own reality.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Her campaign is absurdly mild sweater awareness

jokes.text: We're dreaming together / We're sleeping together / But not like that
jokes.setup: Harris and Brett are expressing their emotional connection through shared dreaming.
jokes.punchline: They spontaneously begin singing a song about their friendship, then clarify 'but not like that' — preemptively defending their platonic bond.
jokes.explanation: The spontaneous song is a great absurdist beat, and 'but not like that' as the clarifying lyric is funny because it suggests the song was going somewhere they needed to preempt. Good self-aware absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: A political apology is like unpleasant medicine. You know you need it, but it tastes terrible going down.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Speaking of which, I need a drink before I go to Leslie's house.

jokes.text: Can you tell us anything else about this ghost? It didn't like me, but that's just 'cause I got a soul of a Ghostbuster.
jokes.setup: Ron, still treating the ghost story as useful evidence, asks a follow-up question.
jokes.punchline: Brett explains the ghost's hostility by reference to his Ghostbuster soul — a piece of self-mythology that is completely earnest and completely insane.
jokes.explanation: 'I got a soul of a Ghostbuster' is a great Brett line — he has a complete spiritual self-conception that includes occupational ghost-fighting heritage. Ron's treatment of this as a legitimate line of inquiry adds to the absurdism.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: You just apologize. It's like alcohol — it solves all your problems.

jokes.text: It said something about how it was worried Brett was gonna mug it. Okay. So we're looking for a racist ghost with black hair who likes shoeshines.
jokes.setup: Harris adds that the ghost was worried Brett would mug it.
jokes.punchline: Ron synthesizes the clues into a description — 'a racist ghost with black hair who likes shoeshines' — as if compiling a normal witness description, treating the ghost's racism as just another data point.
jokes.explanation: Ron's deadpan synthesis of absurd ghost evidence into a clinical description is an excellent joke. 'A racist ghost with black hair who likes shoeshines' is a funny object — it treats ghostly racism as a mundane character trait and packs it efficiently. The structure (Ron treating a ghost investigation like a police briefing) is strong. High economy and quotability.

dialogue.speaker: Jen
dialogue.line: Apologizing is like taking tequila. At first it makes you feel terrible, then you do it over and over, and then you blackout and... wait, no. I'm thinking of my life.

jokes.text: Okay. So we're looking for a racist ghost with black hair who likes shoeshines.
jokes.setup: Ron synthesizes the boys' description of the ghost (April) into a profile.
jokes.punchline: 'Racist ghost' — because the ghost would only talk to Harris, not Brett — is Ron's logical but hilariously clinical conclusion.
jokes.explanation: Ron's investigative summary — completely deadpan — is one of the episode's best lines. The logic is airtight given the absurd premises, and 'racist ghost' as the clinical descriptor is perfectly unexpected. Ron treating this as a valid profile is peak character comedy. Earns 8+: economy is near-perfect, character integration is complete, highly quotable.

jokes.text: You fell in the river reaching for a burrito. Yes, ma'am. That was not one of my finer moments.
jokes.setup: April is questioning Garry about a past incident where he claimed to be mugged.
jokes.punchline: The truth is revealed: Garry fell in a river trying to grab a floating burrito. His modest understatement ('not one of my finer moments') about this absurd incident is very Garry.
jokes.explanation: The burrito-in-the-river reveal is a great Garry backstory. The specificity of falling into a river while reaching for a floating burrito, combined with Garry's quiet acknowledgment ('not one of my finer moments'), is the right comedic register. It's absurd and sad and very Garry all at once.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I love you. Woof woof.

jokes.text: Probably gonna get an earful when I get home tonight. Gayle might even call me the B-word. 'Bozo.'
jokes.setup: Garry anticipates consequences from Gayle for losing his ring.
jokes.punchline: The B-word turns out to be 'Bozo' — a deflation of any adult expectation, and another data point that Gayle's vocabulary of reproach is extremely mild.
jokes.explanation: The B-word misdirection is a textbook misdirection joke executed perfectly. The setup ('the B-word') primes an adult expletive; the reveal ('Bozo') is maximally anti-climactic and consistent with the running Gayle-has-a-sweet-vocabulary joke. The callback to prior Gayle characterization adds resonance. Economy is very high — two words land the punchline. Justifies the 8.0 craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I'm going to vomit.

jokes.text: Wow. We are very different people.
jokes.setup: Donna hears Garry describe 'Bozo' as the worst thing Gayle calls him.
jokes.punchline: Donna's flat assessment — 'we are very different people' — contrasts her own presumably more colorful domestic vocabulary with Garry's gentle household.
jokes.explanation: Five words, maximum implication. Donna's response implies entire worlds about her own domestic life without saying anything explicit. The character contrast between Donna's worldly, assertive personality and Garry's gentle domesticity is perfectly encapsulated. Very economical.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie is her own person. She makes her own decisions. I would never try to control her or tell her what to do.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Now if you'll excuse me, I need to call her and tell her what to wear to this event.

jokes.text: This is my pecan pie recipe. Straight from my Mema's kitchen. Mema was no Leslie Knope. She didn't have a PhD, but she sure knew a lot about P-l-E.
jokes.setup: June Hartwell is doing a talking head segment, positioning her pie recipe as superior to Leslie's approach.
jokes.punchline: She spells out 'PIE' while criticizing Leslie's PhD — an inadvertent self-parody of the Pie Mary's infantilizing premise, delivered with complete sincerity.
jokes.explanation: June spelling out P-I-E while contrasting it with a PhD is unintentionally perfect satire of the episode's central theme. The joke is that June thinks this is a devastating point, while the audience understands she's illustrating exactly why the Pie Mary is retrograde. Strong earned comedy because June is completely earnest.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: Leslie is completely dependent on me for everything. She can't make a single decision without my input.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: What?!

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: No, wait, I meant... Leslie is completely independent. She makes her own decisions.

jokes.text: It's actually Ms. Knope. And actually, right now it's Mr. Wyatt.
jokes.setup: The MC introduces 'Mrs. Wyatt' — Ben, dressed as Leslie's proxy.
jokes.punchline: Leslie corrects the title (Ms. not Mrs.) and then Ben corrects the name to Mr. Wyatt — a cascade of corrections that makes the moment both feminist and absurdist.
jokes.explanation: A good double-correction beat. Leslie's 'Ms.' correction is expected; Ben's 'Mr. Wyatt' follow-up lands the real joke by flipping the gender. The cascade structure works well and efficiently delivers the episode's central comedic premise.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Look, I don't have time to address every made-up movement. Men's rights? That's not a thing. You already have rights. You have all of them.

jokes.text: Now, pack your suitcases, because we're going to a little town called Napoli... In Italy.
jokes.setup: Ben is introducing his calzone entry to the Pie Mary crowd.
jokes.punchline: His dramatic geography lesson ('a little town called Napoli... In Italy') is very Ben — he can't help over-explaining and adding unnecessary context, even when presenting to a contest audience.
jokes.explanation: The parenthetical '... In Italy' after 'a little town called Napoli' is a Ben Wyatt signature — he assumes the audience might not know where Naples is, so he adds the continent. The dramatic buildup to a piece of basic geography is endearing nerd-dad energy.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: Stop asking women if they can have it all.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: STOP asking women if they can have it all.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: STOP ASKING WOMEN IF THEY CAN HAVE IT ALL.

jokes.text: Excuse me, free me from what? From the tyranny of women. We are the Male Men.
jokes.setup: A men's rights group appears at the Pie Mary chanting 'Free Ben Wyatt.'
jokes.punchline: Ben, who voluntarily entered the contest, asks what he's being freed from. The answer: 'the tyranny of women.' 'Male Men' as the group's name is also a comedic goldmine.
jokes.explanation: The Men's Rights group is a sharply constructed satire. Ben's genuine confusion ('free me from what?') is the right protagonist reaction. 'The Male Men' as a group name is funny in its redundancy. The speed at which the episode generates absurd opposing factions (IOW, Male Men, Brandi Maxxxx) is itself a comedic device. Good earned comedy through character consistency.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Sometimes I don't miss them. There, I said it. I'm a horrible mother.

jokes.text: Behind every successful woman is a man she has oppressed.
jokes.setup: The Male Men are protesting Leslie forcing Ben to bake.
jokes.punchline: A subversion of 'behind every successful man is a woman' — the inversion makes their grievance absurdly grandiose and self-pitying simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The inversion of 'behind every successful man is a woman' is clean and economical satire. It's the exact kind of grievance reframing that MRA groups engage in, and the show skewers it efficiently. High quotability and good structure. The absurdity of this applied to Ben voluntarily making calzones elevates it.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie
dialogue.line: You know what? I don't actually know the answer to that.

dialogue.speaker: Ben
dialogue.line: It's Peru.

jokes.text: He has five personalized aprons. Oh. So I guess he was asking for it because of the way he was dressed?
jokes.setup: Leslie insists Ben loves to cook; the Male Men leader implies he was forced.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's comeback — 'So I guess he was asking for it because of the way he was dressed?' — is a pointed inversion of victim-blaming rhetoric applied to a man in an apron.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best jokes. Leslie weaponizes the language of victim-blaming rhetoric by applying it to Ben wearing an apron — making the absurdity of the Male Men's argument vivid. The line is fast, sharp, and devastating. It works on multiple levels: feminist critique, character comedy (Leslie is quick and smart), and pure wit. The setup (Ben has five personalized aprons) makes it perfectly grounded. Justifies the 8.4 craft — this is comparable to the 8.0 anchor example in sharpness.

dialogue.speaker: Random protester
dialogue.line: Let Ben speak! Let Ben speak!

dialogue.speaker: Another protester
dialogue.line: He already spoke.

dialogue.speaker: Random protester
dialogue.line: Let Ben speak! Let Ben speak!

dialogue.speaker: Man with bike
dialogue.line: I've been having bike trouble. What'd I miss?

jokes.text: We are sick and tired of this feminized society. Men have had a very rough go of it, for... Just recently.
jokes.setup: The Male Men leader is articulating their grievance.
jokes.punchline: His historical framing collapses: he starts to claim men have had it hard for a long time, then self-corrects to 'just recently' — an accidental admission of the thinness of the grievance.
jokes.explanation: The pause and self-correction — 'Men have had a very rough go of it, for... Just recently.' — is perfectly constructed. The ellipsis is where the joke lives: he nearly claims a long historical pattern and then course-corrects to an honest 'just recently.' It's devastating satire in twelve words. The self-undermining nature of the correction is sharp and very quotable. Justifies the 8.3 craft.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April lost my house key. Do you know what this means?

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That I'm fired?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: It means my security system has already detected the breach and deployed countermeasures. The key is now useless. I've replaced all the locks with ones that only open for a blood test and a constitutional question. She'll never get in.

jokes.text: We can all agree that no one likes Leslie Knope. But the question is, 'Why?' Marcia Langman.
jokes.setup: A TV panel discusses the Leslie Knope controversy.
jokes.punchline: Starting from the premise that 'no one likes Leslie Knope' as an established fact, then asking 'why?' — the host frames the analysis as if the dislike is settled science.
jokes.explanation: A functional media satire joke. The 'we can all agree' framing of a contested premise is a recognizable cable news trope. The appearance of Marcia Langman (a recurring character) as the expert adds a layer for regular viewers.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: I hid the key by that tree because I knew you'd find it. Because you're smart and capable and... or whatever.

jokes.text: Um. Fierce alert. Eat 'em up, honey.
jokes.setup: Marcia Langman, a traditional values activist, is making her anti-feminist point.
jokes.punchline: Her husband Marshall enthusiastically endorses her with 'Fierce alert. Eat 'em up, honey' — using progressive/gay vernacular to cheer on his traditionalist wife, an absurd contrast.
jokes.explanation: Marshall Langman using 'fierce alert' and 'eat 'em up, honey' — vocabulary that has specific cultural associations antithetical to the Langmans' stated values — is a great character joke. It's a recurring Parks and Rec joke about Marshall that lands every time because it's specific and surprising. Very high character integration and economy. Justifies the 8.0.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: April, I respect you. You remind me of myself at your age - cunning, suspicious of authority, willing to bury things in the ground without telling anyone.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: Ron, what are you talking about?

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: I buried gold in the woods in 1987. Never told my first wife. Then I buried more gold in 1993 - different location, different wife. Then in 2001, I buried gold a third time, but I told my second wife about the first burial, not the second. So if she digs up the first one, she'll think that's all of it. Which it's not.

dialogue.speaker: April
dialogue.line: That's... actually impressive.

dialogue.speaker: Ron
dialogue.line: There's a fourth burial site, but I've forgotten where it is. I'm okay with that. It's still there, earning interest in the form of gold appreciation.

jokes.text: No. Absolutely not. Frankly, I don't think she's done enough to distance herself from this misogynistic lunacy.
jokes.setup: The host asks if the panel member is defending Leslie Knope.
jokes.punchline: She's not defending Leslie — she's attacking Leslie from the left for not being feminist ENOUGH. So Leslie is being attacked from all sides simultaneously.
jokes.explanation: The joke is structural: the setup implies a binary (defend or oppose Leslie), but she attacks from an unanticipated third angle. Leslie being condemned from her own ideological allies adds to the episode's comic satire of how impossible it is to do anything right politically.

dialogue.speaker: Leslie Knope
dialogue.line: Thank you so much for supporting me speaking my mind.

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: Of course, that's what I'm here for.

dialogue.speaker: Announcer
dialogue.line: And the Woman of the Year award goes to... Ben Wyatt!

dialogue.speaker: Ben Wyatt
dialogue.line: What? No, no, no. This doesn't make any sense.

jokes.text: What a surprise. The woman is only talking to other women. Can we have one conversation about feminism where men get to be in charge?
jokes.setup: The host introduces Sasha Dunkirk, head of Women Against Feminism.
jokes.punchline: A Male Men member protests that men should be in charge of the feminism conversation — the complaint perfectly illustrates the premise of their own irrelevance to the topic.
jokes.explanation: A clean, fast satire joke. 'Can we have one conversation about feminism where men get to be in charge?' is a self-undermining complaint that states the Male Men's core objection in the most revealing terms possible. High quotability.

jokes.text: I actually agree with him. I don't need your pity.
jokes.setup: The Male Men member says women should let men lead the feminism discussion; the Women Against Feminism rep responds.
jokes.punchline: She agrees with the Male Men (funny irony), but then snaps at him — 'I don't need your pity' — when he presumably reacts with surprise or congratulation, maintaining her anti-coalition position.
jokes.explanation: A precise satirical exchange. The Women Against Feminism rep agreeing with a Male Men member only to immediately reject his approval ('I don't need your pity') is a perfect encapsulation of the incoherence of anti-feminist positions that still resist male authority. Very efficient double-beat joke.

jokes.text: Joan, Leslie Knope and I are united Oh. In our disgust of this week's events. Leslie, if you're watching, I, Brandi Maxxxx, star of 69 Jump Street and Fifty Shaved Old Gays, have your back.
jokes.setup: A TV panel segment introduces another commentator: Brandi Maxxxx, the adult film star who is a recurring Parks character.
jokes.punchline: Her film titles — '69 Jump Street' and 'Fifty Shaved Old Gays' — are the punchline, adult film parodies of mainstream titles delivered with complete sincerity as credentials.
jokes.explanation: 'Fifty Shaved Old Gays' is genuinely inspired. The parody titles are funny on their own and the fact that Brandi introduces them as professional credentials elevates the joke. Parks and Rec gets significant mileage from Brandi's recurring sincerity. 'Fifty Shaved Old Gays' in particular has strong quotability.

jokes.text: Oof. You really stepped in it this time, Knope. Told ya. Being a candidate's wife is a tough gig.
jokes.setup: Jen watches the news coverage turn into total chaos.
