jokes.punchline: Jen's casual 'told ya' — referencing her earlier cynical predictions — is delivered with comfortable satisfaction at being proven right.
jokes.explanation: A functional callback. Jen's satisfaction at being right is character-appropriate but the joke doesn't add much beyond confirming the callback.

jokes.text: Because June Hartwell is a lukewarm bowl of nothing. She started an awareness campaign called 'Bring a Sweater.' She calls it 'goose bump prevention.'
jokes.setup: Leslie asks why the other candidate's wife isn't being scrutinized like she is.
jokes.punchline: 'A lukewarm bowl of nothing' is a devastatingly good insult, and it's followed by the evidence: Bring a Sweater / goose bump prevention is a campaign so mild it barely constitutes a thought.
jokes.explanation: 'A lukewarm bowl of nothing' is one of the best insults in the episode, possibly the series. The temperature-based noun phrase is evocative, specific, and devastating. The follow-up evidence (Bring a Sweater / goose bump prevention) is perfect: it's funny precisely because it's such a low-stakes, not-quite-wrong initiative. 'Goose bump prevention' as the campaign's alternative name is almost too earnest to be real, which is why it's so funny. Justifies the 8.4.

jokes.text: Feminists and pie makers united for equality despite our philosophies on equal rights and crust flakiness.
jokes.setup: Leslie is proposing a new political coalition to manage the pie controversy.
jokes.punchline: The parallel structure — equal rights AND crust flakiness as equivalent policy disputes between the groups — is the joke. Leslie treating crust flakiness as a legitimate ideological divide is very Leslie.
jokes.explanation: The juxtaposition of 'equal rights' and 'crust flakiness' as parallel ideological disputes is a sharp absurdist joke that's completely believable as something Leslie would say. She genuinely thinks crust flakiness is a substantive policy distinction worth acknowledging in coalition-building. Good economy and character integration.

jokes.text: Just ignore the fact that you're right, put on your blandest outfit... So that one, hopefully, and then just go out there and publicly apologize. Done.
jokes.setup: Jen is advising Leslie on how to handle the controversy.
jokes.punchline: Jen's three-step solution — ignore being right, wear the blandest outfit (she gestures at Leslie's current outfit, implying it's already bland), publicly apologize — is delivered as a perfectly reasonable campaign management protocol.
jokes.explanation: 'So that one, hopefully' — Jen gesturing at Leslie's current outfit as an example of 'bland' — is a nice visual beat (inferred). The cynicism of 'ignore the fact that you're right' as step one of political crisis management is sharp Jen character work.

jokes.text: It's like taking a shot of tequila. You just gotta force it down, suddenly the world feels so much more pleasant. I do three shots every time I have to enter this house.
jokes.setup: Jen is advising Leslie to just apologize and move on, even if it feels bad.
jokes.punchline: The tequila analogy is extended to reveal that Jen has a three-shot protocol specifically for entering Leslie's house — a callback to the earlier sticky-house joke and a revelation about Jen's coping mechanisms.
jokes.explanation: The callback lands excellently. The tequila analogy sets up a good-natured observation, then the punchline reveals that Jen has a three-shot pre-entry ritual for Leslie's house specifically — connecting back to the sticky-house joke from the episode's opening. The absurdity of a three-shot commitment just to walk into someone's home is funny and the callback adds resonance. Justifies the 8.0.

jokes.text: First off, I got a dude in maintenance to open up that grate this morning. So here's your rings, keys, credit cards, and I found some heart medicine I assume is yours?
jokes.setup: Donna arrives with a resolution to the grate catastrophe.
jokes.punchline: The escalating list of recovered items climaxes with 'heart medicine' — Donna's casual, unprompted assumption about the heart medicine's ownership is both practical and darkly funny.
jokes.explanation: The heart medicine addition to the recovery list is a good escalating detail — Garry's situation has apparently been more medically fraught than we knew. Donna's casual assumption ('I assume is yours?') is appropriately deadpan.

jokes.text: Also, I thought I'd bring over some fresh oranges for you and Gayle.
jokes.setup: Earlier, Garry described that when Gayle is mad, she makes him go for 'fresh oranges for the morning OJ.'
jokes.punchline: Donna brings Garry oranges, preemptively addressing the Gayle consequence — showing she was paying attention and actually cares about Garry.
jokes.explanation: A warm callback that pays off the orange detail from earlier. Donna's gesture reveals genuine affection for Garry beneath her usual teasing. The callback rewards attentive viewers and lands as both funny and touching — a Parks and Rec specialty.

jokes.text: And I just wanna thank you for taking me down memory lane, ya big B-word. 'Buddy.'
jokes.setup: Donna is saying goodbye to Garry warmly.
jokes.punchline: The B-word callback — this time from Donna, who reveals her B-word is also 'Buddy' — pays off the running joke with an unexpected warmth. Donna's B-word is no more profane than Gayle's.
jokes.explanation: An outstanding callback payoff. The joke at 15:51 established that Gayle's B-word is 'Bozo' — undermining the expectation of profanity. This callback doubles down: Donna, whom we'd expect to have a colorful vocabulary, also reveals her B-word is 'Buddy.' The warmth and the structural mirroring of the two B-word reveals are perfect. 'Ya big Buddy' from Donna to Garry is unexpectedly affecting and very funny. Justifies the 8.4.

jokes.text: So much has changed around here. I just wanted to remember the good old days, when a shoeshine was two bits, and there were no Mexicans in the music business.
jokes.setup: An elderly councilman has been sitting at the old shoeshine stand reminiscing.
jokes.punchline: '...and there were no Mexicans in the music business' — an unexpected racist non sequitur that reveals the councilman's nostalgic filter is deeply problematic.
jokes.explanation: A dark subversive joke with the structure of a perfectly innocent nostalgia monologue that suddenly veers into blatant prejudice. The specific target ('the music business') is slightly more absurd than a generic racist statement, which makes it funny as satire of a type of casual historical bigotry. The joke requires the audience to simultaneously recognize and laugh at the ugliness of the sentiment.

jokes.text: 'Hi Andy, I hate people, but you are okay. It's weird. Woof, woof. April.'
jokes.setup: They find a note from past-April hidden at the shoeshine stand.
jokes.punchline: Past-April's note to Andy is the most April love letter imaginable: 'I hate people, but you are okay. It's weird.' followed by 'Woof, woof.' It's tender and deeply strange.
jokes.explanation: This is the best joke in the episode. The note is a perfect character artifact: April's love declaration is filtered entirely through her personality — she can't say she likes someone without starting with 'I hate people.' The 'It's weird' addendum is both April's discomfort with affection and an honest expression of her confusion. 'Woof, woof' as a sign-off is pure April — absurd, animal, inexplicable, and somehow intimate. The economy is extraordinary: 22 words reveal a complete emotional portrait. This is the kind of joke that makes you love a character more. Character integration is essentially perfect — no one else could have written this note. Justifies the 9.0.

jokes.text: My God, babe, you were so into me. That's hilarious. We're married. Still.
jokes.setup: Andy reads April's past love note with delight.
jokes.punchline: April's 'Still.' — a callback to the earlier 'Still.' at 10:52 — is deployed again here, doubling as a callback and a character confirmation.
jokes.explanation: A second deployment of 'Still.' as April's response to the embarrassment of being married to someone you had a crush on. It works as a callback and as a character moment — April's mortification at her own past feelings is consistent and funny. Good economy.

jokes.text: It's a dead end. No more clues. See me in my office. If it makes you feel any better, I had a big crush on you too. That does make me feel a little better. Thanks.
jokes.setup: The puzzle has apparently reached a dead end; April is dejected. Ron's response is unexpected.
jokes.punchline: Ron admits he had a big crush on April (as a protégé/mentee) — the language of romantic crushes applied to professional admiration is both funny and moving. April's sincere 'That does make me feel a little better. Thanks.' completes the joke.
jokes.explanation: A great Ron/April moment that uses 'crush' in the professional mentor sense, which is slightly unusual language that reveals Ron's genuine feeling without breaking his emotional reserve. April's response — not moved to tears, just mildly comforted — is exactly right for her character too. The warmth and the slight awkwardness are perfectly calibrated. High character integration for both. Justifies the 8.3.

jokes.text: Oh! Thank God. Get off my boat!
jokes.setup: Ron discovers something (presumably the key, at the boat — inferred from context and the episode's resolution).
jokes.punchline: Ron's 'Get off my boat!' suggests he has a boat, that it was being occupied, and that he's more focused on clearing his boat than on the key itself. Very Ron.
jokes.explanation: Ron having a boat is consistent with his character (man of the outdoors, solitary pursuits). 'Get off my boat!' as the lead exclamation — prioritizing territorial privacy over relief at the puzzle's resolution — is very Ron. Quick character beat.

jokes.text: Good afternoon. I'm here today to share with you all my vision for the economic future of Southern Indiana. But first, Leslie Knope, my wife, has a brief statement.
jokes.setup: Ben is supposed to be giving his economic address.
jokes.punchline: Ben immediately sidelines himself to give Leslie the platform — inverting the episode's premise where Leslie has been sidelined for Ben's campaign.
jokes.explanation: The structural reversal is the joke — Ben using his platform to give Leslie hers. Functional and thematically satisfying, though the comedy is more structural than line-level.

jokes.text: I love how independent my wife is, and because of that, I will not let her speak. That came out wrong.
jokes.setup: Ben is stepping in to defend Leslie at the press event.
jokes.punchline: 'I will not let her speak' — Ben's declaration of Leslie's independence immediately results in silencing her, which he immediately recognizes. 'That came out wrong' is the correct and funny acknowledgment.
jokes.explanation: A structurally perfect joke. The setup is Ben declaring Leslie's independence; the punchline is that his method of declaring it is to prevent her from speaking — an immediate, complete self-contradiction. 'That came out wrong' is exactly the right three-word acknowledgment, delivered with perfect timing. The joke is funny, the recognition is faster than most of these moments, and the character work (Ben well-intentioned and immediately aware of his error) is strong. Justifies the 8.1.

jokes.text: Second, the Male Men... Where are you? Ah. You're ridiculous, and men's rights is nothing.
jokes.setup: Leslie is giving an organized speech addressing various controversies, including the Male Men group.
jokes.punchline: She has to locate the Male Men in the crowd before dismissing them — and then her dismissal ('men's rights is nothing') is delivered with complete calm.
jokes.explanation: A good structured takedown. The pause to locate the Male Men in the crowd before addressing them adds physical comedy (inferred). 'Men's rights is nothing' delivered with the same administrative calm as her other points is very Leslie — she's treating this like a meeting agenda item.

jokes.text: 'Why did I change my hairstyle?' Oh, I don't know. I just thought it would look better. Or my kids got gum in it.
jokes.setup: Leslie is pre-answering all the sexist questions she'll face in the campaign.
jokes.punchline: The hairstyle question's answer — either aesthetic choice OR a child-related emergency — is a perfectly mundane pair of reasons that reveals the question's absurdity.
jokes.explanation: 'Or my kids got gum in it' is the joke — a completely plausible, parent-specific alternate explanation for a hairstyle change that reveals the irrelevance of the question. The callback to gum as a household hazard (earlier sticky house jokes) may be intentional.

jokes.text: 'Are you trying to have it all?' That question makes no sense. It's a stupid question. Stop asking it. Don't ask it.
jokes.setup: Leslie continues pre-answering campaign questions, addressing 'are you trying to have it all?'
jokes.punchline: Her escalating dismissal — 'makes no sense,' 'stupid question,' 'stop asking it,' 'don't ask it' — is four ways of saying the same thing, each slightly more irritated, which is very Leslie when she's frustrated.
jokes.explanation: Leslie's four-step dismissal is a good character joke — she keeps re-saying it because she's working through her irritation in real time. The escalation from 'no sense' to 'don't ask it' mirrors her emotional state.

jokes.text: And by the way, no one's ever asked me that question. No one asks me, 'Where are your kids?' Or, 'Who's taking care of them?' By the way, who is taking care of the kids right now? My mom, babe. Everything's fine.
jokes.setup: Leslie points out that Ben is never asked about childcare.
jokes.punchline: Leslie's feminist point is immediately illustrated by the fact that she doesn't know where her own kids are right now — and Ben does, because he arranged it.
jokes.explanation: A structurally excellent joke with real thematic resonance. Leslie makes the feminist point that no one asks men about childcare — and then in the very next breath asks where her kids are because she genuinely doesn't know. Ben's calm 'My mom, babe. Everything's fine' is the perfect deadpan resolution. The joke simultaneously makes a real point and gently shows that Leslie, in the middle of her speech, really did need to ask. The self-undermining irony is beautifully earned. Justifies the 8.1.

jokes.text: I'd say that's fifty-fifty boos and cheers. Yeah. That seems about right.
jokes.setup: Leslie's speech has concluded and the crowd is audibly split.
jokes.punchline: Jen's deadpan assessment of the 50/50 reaction — and Ben's quick agreement — treats a politically divided crowd response as a satisfactory outcome.
jokes.explanation: A quick, satisfying capper to the speech scene. Jen's calm assessment of the 50/50 split as an acceptable result is funny because it lowers the bar for success — and Ben agreeing makes it a two-person deadpan beat.

jokes.text: Let Ben speak! Let Ben speak! He just spoke. Oh. Sorry. I just got here. I had a broken bike chain. My bad.
jokes.setup: After both Leslie and Ben have spoken, a Male Men member starts chanting 'Let Ben speak!'
jokes.punchline: He's arrived late and missed the entire speech — his advocacy is completely moot, and his explanation (broken bike chain) is an anti-climactic human detail.
jokes.explanation: A very funny capper to the Male Men thread. The protest is rendered completely pointless by his late arrival; 'He just spoke' is the devastating reply; and 'I had a broken bike chain. My bad.' is the human detail that makes it real. The deflation is complete and the specificity of the bike chain explanation is perfect. The joke works structurally and as character comedy.

jokes.text: So I guess we are celebrating that you trusted me and I let you down. Great. I change my house locks every 16 days. That key has been useless since the second Tuesday after I gave it to you.
jokes.setup: April is upset that the key was ultimately useless; Ron has a response.
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he changes his locks every 16 days — making the entire episode's MacGuffin (the key) functionally worthless from nearly the start. The specificity of 'the second Tuesday' is very Ron.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's two or three best jokes and a structural masterpiece. The entire B-plot has been a hunt for a key that would give access to Ron's house. The reveal that Ron changes his locks every 16 days — with the precision of 'the second Tuesday after I gave it to you' — retroactively makes the whole quest meaningless while being completely and perfectly in character for Ron. Of course Ron changes his locks every 16 days. Of course he knows exactly when it became useless. The joke is simultaneously a great anti-climax and a character revelation. 'Second Tuesday' as the specific unit is Ron's precision turned to paranoid self-protection. Justifies the 8.9.

jokes.text: What matters is that I trust you and admire you as a person. I will be sorry to see you leave this town. For many reasons. Not the least of which is that you created a puzzle that even I couldn't solve.
jokes.setup: Ron is giving April an emotional send-off as she prepares to move to Washington.
jokes.punchline: Among Ron's reasons for regretting April's departure, the puzzle she accidentally created — a puzzle 'even I couldn't solve' — ranks as a significant factor. This is Ron's emotional vocabulary.
jokes.explanation: Ron's compliment is that April accidentally created a puzzle he couldn't solve — for Ron, this is a profound compliment, possibly the highest he can give. It ties back to the cold open (Ron solving the Puzzlers' Guild hunt instantly) to give this emotional beat real resonance. The fact that Ron lists this alongside genuine admiration ('trust you and admire you as a person') reveals that, for Ron, intellectual achievement and character achievement are equivalent. A very warm, funny, character-perfect moment. Justifies the 8.3.

jokes.text: And boy, oh, boy, did you love Andy. 'Woof, woof.' It really is embarrassing.
jokes.setup: Ron has just delivered a warm send-off to April.
jokes.punchline: He can't resist one last tease about April's old crush on Andy, citing the 'woof, woof' note — April's confirmation that 'it really is embarrassing' lands as a good capper.
jokes.explanation: A good callback that lets Ron punctuate the emotional scene with characteristic deflection — he's moved, but he'll tease. 'Woof, woof' as the quoted evidence is funny because it's such a strange thing to quote back at someone. April's 'It really is embarrassing' is the correct response.

jokes.text: 'Woof, woof.' Bark. Why here? Because this tree reminds me of you. It's strong. And quiet. And always here when you need it. Or whatever.
jokes.setup: April has remembered where the key is — buried under a tree — and the reason she chose it.
jokes.punchline: 'Because this tree reminds me of you. It's strong. And quiet. And always here when you need it.' is a genuinely touching tribute — and then April immediately undercuts it with 'Or whatever.' The self-rescue from sincerity is classic April.
jokes.explanation: One of the episode's best moments. April's tribute to Ron — delivered through a tree, which is very April — is 'strong, quiet, always here when you need it.' It's a beautiful description of what Ron is to her. And then 'Or whatever.' rescues her from sentimentality in the most April way possible. The two-word escape hatch ('Or whatever') is one of the most efficient comedy beats in the episode. The joke is warm AND funny AND deeply character-specific. 'Woof, woof / Bark' as the trigger for the memory is an elegant callback. Justifies the 8.7.

jokes.text: I have always felt a certain kinship with April, and this is proof that I was correct. Not the nice things she said about me, the fact that I buried a large amount of gold under that same tree years ago. I have since moved it. Or have I? Or was I lying the whole time? Or was I lying about lying? Or was there never any gold to begin with? Or...
jokes.setup: Ron gives a talking-head confessional about the tree that April chose to hide his key.
jokes.punchline: Ron reveals he also buried gold there — then immediately begins a recursive series of denials and re-denials about whether the gold exists or ever existed, ending on an unresolved 'Or...'
jokes.explanation: The episode's best joke and a Ron Swanson masterpiece. The confessional establishes kinship through gold-hoarding — completely believable. Then 'I have since moved it. Or have I? Or was I lying the whole time? Or was I lying about lying? Or was there never any gold to begin with? Or...' is a recursive truth-deconstruction that is simultaneously absurdist, self-mythologizing, and deeply Ron. Ron doesn't just have secrets — he weaponizes uncertainty itself. The escalating 'or...' structure is perfectly constructed, each level adding another layer of epistemic chaos. The final unresolved 'Or...' leaves the audience in Ron's preferred state: total informational darkness. Character integration is essentially perfect — only Ron Swanson would do this, and he would do exactly this. Justifies the 8.9.

jokes.text: Congratulations, Ben Wyatt, you are this year's IOW Woman of the Year. Son of a bitch.
jokes.setup: Elise returns to tell Leslie they loved her speech and especially how Ben gave her a platform.
jokes.punchline: The Woman of the Year award — which Leslie desperately wanted for herself — goes to Ben. Leslie's 'Son of a bitch' is the perfect reaction.
jokes.explanation: A near-perfect structural joke that serves as the episode's comedic climax. The callback to Leslie's Woman of the Year aspiration (complete with pre-written speech) is perfectly paid off: the award goes to Ben for giving Leslie a platform. The irony is multiple-layered: (1) Leslie desperately wanted this award, (2) it goes to her husband, (3) it goes to him for supporting her, (4) this means a man won the Woman of the Year award, which the IOW seems entirely comfortable with. Leslie's 'Son of a bitch' is the precisely correct reaction — one beat, maximum frustration, deeply Leslie. Justifies the 8.8.

tmdb_overview: Leslie and Ben come under fire for participating in an old Pawnee tradition. April and Ron go on a scavenger hunt. Donna and Garry stroll down memory lane.
insight: Late-season Parks hits 77 jokes in 31 minutes despite declining emotional stakes.
